s01.slug: MONDAY · 8:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DESK
body: The Fishbowl TV is on CNN with the sound down to a murmur, and in Berlin it’s ten to six and already dark. The Brandenburg Gate is lit gold, and running away from it along the line where the Wall used to stand is a mile of giant foam dominoes, each one taller than a man and painted by schoolkids from everywhere — a dove, a Trabant, a fist, a sun in sunglasses. Every one of them is still standing. The crawl says somebody gives the first one a shove tonight, Berlin time. In California that’s late morning. Jack will be sitting in a lecture hall when the twentieth century falls over again.
Priya catches him between the front desk and the door. She has her clipboard flat against her chest and, held out at arm’s length in her other hand, a pink envelope.
“Housing sends RAs the hold list,” she says, “and I’m supposed to *facilitate a conversation*.” She puts it in his hand. “This is me facilitating.”

body.title: RESIDENTIAL SERVICES — NOTICE OF BALANCE DUE
body.text:
SPRING 2010 HOUSING · COSTIGAN, JOHN A. · DELGADO 412
Balance after aid: $340.00
A REGISTRATION HOLD has been placed on your record. Payment or an approved arrangement is due at Residential Services by 5:00 p.m., Friday, November 13.

body: “They make it *pink*?”
“Nobody throws away pink,” says Priya. “There were studies.”
Jack knows what three hundred and forty dollars is: the family share, the line on last spring’s aid letter that was supposed to come from Glenwood Avenue and didn’t.

Priya is still going. Freshman registration opens Monday the sixteenth at seven a.m., and a hold means he can’t; Hale’s spring seminar fills by seven-oh-five. “I watched it happen last year from the circulation desk. A sophomore cried on the returns cart.” She checks something on the clipboard that may or may not concern him. “Unrelated. Circulation lost two overnight people to the swine flu. Midnight to six. Eight-forty an hour. I’m not *recommending* it. I’m informing you it exists.”
“Thanks, Priya.”
“That wasn’t a conversation,” she says, already writing. “I’m logging it as one.”

He takes the stairs back up to four for his bag. Somebody has propped the lounge door with a chair, and over the weekend Margot has wiped the whiteboard to the frame, all but one corner, and lettered it fresh in her square black capitals:

body.title: THE WHITEBOARD, 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body.text:
20 YEARS · WHO BROUGHT IT DOWN?
(DISCUSS. ARGUE. BE WRONG.)
TONIGHT 9 P.M.
In the corner the useful-idiots tally: C 8 · B 7, and under it, in Margot’s smallest capitals, STUPAK: SAME SIDE (BOTH).

body: In 412 the blinds are down and Theo is asleep on his face with one bare foot off the mattress. Jack finds Hale’s reader on the desk and opens it to the page where he quit last night. He lays the pink envelope in along the spine, creases it once with his thumb so the corner won’t show, and folds the reader shut on it.

journal.title: The hold
journal.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists.

body.text: → Jack Costigan: mom sent u something!!! newman desk. DONT OPEN IT WITHOUT ME

body: Jack reads it at half past four on the Dell with his bag still on his shoulder, and types *I won’t* under it, and posts it. By the time he has the bag off, two people like that too.

Theo comes in behind him with a paper cup from the UCen, looking for somewhere to set it down, and what he settles on is the reader on the corner of Jack’s desk, which is fatter on one side than the other. The cup tips. Theo saves the cup, and the pink envelope slides out across the blotter and stops against his wrist.
Theo never looks for anything. Things present themselves to Theo. He reads this one upside down.
“How much?”
“Doesn’t matter.”
Theo turns it right way up with one finger. “Costigan. I spend that on *parking*.”
“You spend that on parking because you park in the fire lane.”
“I park where the light is good.” He waits.
“No,” Jack says.
“You’re the only man I know who’s proud of being broke. It’s very Steinbeck.”
“Steinbeck got paid.”
“Steinbeck had a *publisher*, Costigan. You have me.” He waits again, longer. Jack goes on unlacing his boots.
Theo gives it a minute. Then he slides the envelope back into the reader at the same page and lines the reader up with the corner of the desk, exactly where it was, and takes his hand away.
“The offer has no expiration date.”
He carries his coffee to his bed and lies down on top of the duvet in his loafers. Every so often Theo turns a page of *Variety*, sooner than anybody could have read it.

CNN is running it again for the West Coast. On the lounge TV a gray-haired man with a famous mustache puts his hands on the first giant domino down at the Potsdamer Platz end and shoves, and it tips into the next one, and the next, and the painted mile of them goes down along the line where the Wall stood, toward the lit Gate — doves, flags, a Trabant with tulips coming out of the tailpipe — one push and every one of them flat. The crowd in Berlin roars like it’s 1989. On the couch under the set Doug Pruitt is asleep with a forearm over his eyes and misses the end of Communism entirely.

body.text: The court-bouillon is on the counter by the microwave in the dented Newman stockpot, Saturday’s rockfish out of Rudy’s walk-in, the masking tape still on the lid: LENA’S. MONDAY. FOR THE HARBOR INN. Dulce and Rosario got theirs at six. Lena ladles Jack a bowl of what’s left and hands it to him with a spoon. “Something to argue over,” she says. “Eat while I take you apart.”

body: Margot has the marker uncapped and the board divided into columns with a ruler she brought from her room. Kevin, in a navy quarter-zip, is timekeeper, as always, with the stopwatch up on his BlackBerry. Theo is draped over the arm of the good chair with a mug of something Italian. Laney has the chair itself, legs folded under her, with a pint of Cherry Garcia and a spoon she uses for emphasis. Becca is across campus at Portolá with a Bio 1A problem set due at eight. Lena sits on the carpet with her back against the couch, in the oatmeal cardigan, sleeves already shoved to the elbow and a Bic in her fist.

body.title: 4th-floor lounge whiteboard
body.text:
WHO BROUGHT IT DOWN?
GORBACHEV (LINDQVIST) · THE POPE (COSTIGAN) · A UNION (BROUSSARD) · HASSELHOFF (VANCE)

body: Margot opens for Gorbachev in forty seconds flat: history’s great men are mostly men who declined to do something catastrophic, and in 1989 Mikhail Gorbachev declined to send the tanks. “Structurally,” she says, “he simply didn’t.” Jack goes for the Pope: Warsaw, June 1979, a million people in Victory Square, and John Paul II asking the Holy Spirit to renew the face of the earth — and then, after a pause the Party heard all the way to Moscow, *the face of this land*.
Theo rises to defend his candidate. “New Year’s Eve, 1989. A crane. A light-up jacket. A scarf made of piano keys.” He spreads his hands. “I’d option it.”
“The Germans, sugar,” Laney says, around her spoon. “They did it with their *hands*.”
Then Lena gets up on her knees on the carpet, and the room settles, because everybody on four knows what that means.

“Gdańsk,” she says. “August 1980. An electrician they fired from the Lenin Shipyard four years before climbs over the fence — *in*, Jack, he climbs *in* — and a year later there’s a union ten million strong, in a country of thirty-five million. Lord have mercy, look who they let push the first domino tonight.” She points the Bic at the TV, where Lech Wałęsa is being shown again, mustache and all, pushing. “The only mass movement in the whole Soviet bloc was a *labor union*, Costigan.”

choices.text: “There was an altar at every gate in Gdańsk. The union was the Church in overalls.”
response: “There was an altar at every gate in Gdańsk,” Jack says. “Mass at the fence every morning of the strike. The Black Madonna wired to the bars and the Pope’s picture next to her. Your union was the Church in overalls.”
Lena doesn’t even let it finish landing. “Then you just agreed with me in Latin.”

choices.text: “He climbed a wall to get in. Ten years later everybody climbed one to get out. Trendsetter.”
response: “So he climbed a wall to get in,” Jack says, “and ten years later everybody climbed one to get out. The man was a trendsetter.”
The lounge laughs. Lena points the Bic at him. “That doesn’t count. A laugh is not a point. I’m a human being, I have *reflexes*.”

choices.text: “Welders and electricians. My father would’ve joined it in a day.”
response: “Welders and electricians,” Jack says. “Guys who punch a clock. My father would’ve joined it in a day.”
Lena stops with the Bic in the air. Whatever she had ready next, she puts it down. “He would have,” she says. “I’d have marched behind him.”

choices.text: “Leipzig. Monday prayers at the Nikolaikirche. October ninth, seventy thousand people carrying candles so their hands were full.”
response: “Leipzig,” Jack says. “Monday prayers for peace at the Nikolaikirche. October ninth, seventy thousand people come out of the church and walk the ring road carrying candles. You carry a candle with one hand and keep it lit with the other.” He holds up both of his, empty. “No hands left for a rock. The Stasi had a plan for rocks.”
Lena opens her mouth and shuts it again. Margot writes LEIPZIG under THE POPE in capitals an inch high.

body: Kevin calls the round. Lena gets to her feet, takes a yellow highlighter out of her cardigan pocket, and draws a pair of golden arches under A UNION, right on Margot’s board. Margot looks at the arches as if they’d been drawn on her personally.

“So the Wall comes down,” Lena says, “and who’s waiting on the other side with open arms? Not the Holy Father. Blue jeans. A McDonald’s. The West showed up with a checkbook and bought whatever was left standing.”

body.text: “Twenty years later — ask your daddy who won. GM took a bailout and he took a pink slip. That’s the market that won, Jack. Same one.”
body.else: “Twenty years later — ask anybody in Michigan who won. GM took a bailout and the line took the pink slips. That’s the market that won, Jack. Same one.”

body: She says it the way she says everything in a fight, fast and with her chin up, and it’s a good argument; it has numbers in it, and a pink slip, and a McDonald’s. Margot, who has no intention of moderating her own debate: “Neither the Pope nor the electrician had an army. Gorbachev had one, and he kept it home.” Theo raises a hand to point out that Hasselhoff, at least, never bought anything, and is ignored by three women at once. Laney says “Well, *damn*,” with real respect, into the Cherry Garcia. Kevin restarts the stopwatch.

choices.text: “The market didn’t build the Wall. It just never needed one.”
response: “The market didn’t build the Wall,” Jack says. “It just never needed one. In Ohio they let you leave.”

response.text: “Tell that to Lordstown,” Lena says. Beside Kevin, Theo, very quietly: “Ooh.” Lena doesn’t take her eyes off Jack.
response.else: “Tell that to Flint,” Lena says. Beside Kevin, Theo, very quietly: “Ooh.” Lena doesn’t take her eyes off Jack.

choices.text: “He’d tell you GM lost. Then he’d tell you the Browns lost worse.”
choices.key: Monday night Lena said your father’s pink slip was the market that won. You gave her the point.
response: “He’d tell you GM lost,” Jack says. “Then he’d tell you the Browns lost worse.”
The lounge laughs, and Lena laughs with it, and points the highlighter at him like a promise. “You tell him I said the Browns are a *structural problem*.”

choices.key: Monday night Lena brought your father into the argument. You told her to leave him out of it.
response: “Leave my father out of it.”
He says it harder than the lounge is built for.
Lena looks at him. Then she lets the line go — drops all of it, GM and the bailout and the pink slip, and he can watch her do it. “All right,” she says, level.
Laney finds something absorbing on the ceiling tiles. Kevin’s thumb hovers over the stopwatch. The room has gone one degree cooler, and the point is Jack’s.

choices.text: “Sindermann, East German Politburo: ‘We planned for everything. Except candles and prayers.’”
response: “Horst Sindermann,” Jack says. “East German Politburo. ‘We had planned for everything. We were prepared for everything. Except candles and prayers.’”
“Source?” says Margot.
“He said it before he died.”
“*Source.*”
On the carpet Lena sits back against the couch and enjoys Margot doing her job for her, thoroughly, with her arms folded.

body: Jack types *candles. praying* with his thumb and shuts the phone. “Final round,” Margot says. “Broussard to close. Be brief. Pruitt has a nine a.m.” On the couch Pruitt does not stir. The third round Lena takes sitting down. Her hand goes to the medal at her collarbone and turns it over once while she works it out, and the lounge waits for her, even Theo.

“Candles in Leipzig,” she says. “A union in Gdańsk. And a Polish pope who was both — a man who worked in a quarry and a chemical plant under the Nazis and came home and said Mass for the people who still did. You want it to be prayer *instead of* bread. It was prayer *and* bread. That’s the whole Church, Jack, and you keep picking one.”

body.text: She says it to the whiteboard more than to him.

response: “Both,” Jack says. “Fine. *Both*.”
Theo groans into his mug. Lena doesn’t gloat. She looks at Jack honestly pleased, as if he’d done something hard on purpose, and the room finds that much harder to take than a victory lap.

choices.text: “Bread doesn’t knock down walls. Seventy thousand candles did.”
response: “Bread doesn’t knock down walls,” Jack says. “Seventy thousand candles did.”
“Candles don’t feed anybody in Gdańsk.”
“They weren’t hungry for bread.”
“Everybody’s hungry for bread, Costigan.” She’s up on her knees again. “Ask a welder.”
“Ask a welder what he prayed for.”
Kevin’s BlackBerry chirps. “Time,” he says, into a silence that could clearly go another hour.

choices.text: “Margot. Write down ‘both.’ Write down I said it first.”
response: “Margot,” Jack says. “Write down ‘both.’ And write down I said it first.”
“A concession with a joke in it is a concession,” says Margot.
Lena laughs — a big unguarded crack of a laugh that makes Doug Pruitt say “*Present*” in his sleep — and she’s still laughing at Jack when Kevin calls time.

choices.text: “What I said about my father. That was me, not the argument.”
response: “What I said about my father,” Jack says. “That was me. It wasn’t the argument.”
“I know it was.” Lena looks at him then, properly, for the first time since he said it. “I’d have said it different if I’d known it was still sore.”

body: Margot stands at the board with the marker, taking her time about it, because she can. Then she writes her verdict across the bottom, under all four columns, in capitals:

BOTH. (UNDERLINED. AGAINST MY WILL.)
+ ONE APOLOGY. ACCEPTED, PER BROUSSARD.

SHE MADE HIM SAY IT.

ASTERISK: THE FATHER THING.

HE WAS WINNING. THEN HE WAS FUNNY.

A CONCESSION WITH A JOKE IN IT IS STILL A CONCESSION.

body: She caps the marker with a click and lays it in the tray, and that is the end of the Cold War on the fourth floor of Delgado Hall. Theo applauds Hasselhoff, alone, for some time.

body.text: Lena goes round collecting the bowls, Jack’s last, and fits the lid back on the Newman stockpot over the masking tape.
“Night, Costigan.” Not *Youngstown*.
body.else: “Go to bed, Youngstown,” Lena says, warm. “You argue worse tired.”

body: Kevin and Laney go out arguing about whether Hasselhoff got a single vote. Margot takes her ruler. The lounge empties one person at a time, and somebody kills the overhead lights on the way out and leaves the TV, and on the screen the dominoes go down again on a loop, a mile of them, over Doug Pruitt asleep on the couch.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 1:04 AM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: The RAZR lights up on the desk at 1:02 and shivers against the reader, and the little outside screen says MOM.

Theo lifts his head off the pillow, looks at the lit phone, and puts his head back down. Jack takes the phone out to the east stairwell in his socks, the Carhartt over his T-shirt, and climbs to the third step above the fourth-floor landing, where the one bar lives, and holds the RAZR up toward the sprinkler head. “Ma.”

It’s four in the morning on Glenwood Avenue, and his mother is very calm. Maria Costigan yells about the cardoons and the Browns and the price of stamps; she goes calm for hospitals and wakes. He sits down on the step, the concrete cold through his socks, and puts his free hand over his other ear against the fluorescent hum. “Okay,” he says. “Okay. Tell me.”

The SUB pay ended last week, she says — the last check. She didn’t tell him, because what was he going to do about it from California. Tonight his father went down to the bar on Midlothian for the Monday game, the Steelers in Denver — “and he doesn’t even *like* the Steelers, Jack” — and the bar closed at two-thirty. It’s after four. The truck isn’t back. His cell phone is on the counter by the toaster; she knows because she called it, and it rang in the kitchen.

Nonna is at the kitchen table with her rosary. She went dizzy on the stairs Sunday and has slept in the chair in the front room since, but tonight she won’t go to the chair. Gina is up too, on the landing, where she thinks nobody can see her.
“I’m not calling the police on your father, Jack,” his mother says. “I’m calling you.”

choices.key: At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You prayed the Sorrowful Mysteries with her until the truck pulled in.
response: “Let’s pray it, Ma.”

It’s already Tuesday in Youngstown, which makes them the Sorrowful Mysteries. She has her beads out by the time he’s said so; he can hear them on the tabletop. The Agony in the Garden. Partway into the second decade Nonna comes in from the other side of the kitchen in Italian, a syllable behind them and sure of every word — *Santa Maria, Madre di Dio* — and nobody corrects anybody. They’re on the Crowning with Thorns when it comes.

At 4:51 Eastern — nine minutes to two here, the stairwell bright and empty around him — his mother stops in the middle of a word. Headlights, across her kitchen window. Then, down the line from twenty-four hundred miles, a hollow bang and the long rattle of a trash can rolling at the curb, and the Silverado’s bad muffler, and the engine cut.
“He’s home,” she says. “Go to sleep, honey.” And then, because it has been on her list since August: “The spring thing. For your room. We’ll find it.”
“I’ve got it, Ma.”

She goes out with the cordless. He hears the storm door, and the cold of the driveway coming into the phone, and his father’s voice, too low for words, and the storm door again. When she comes back on, she says it quietly. “He sat in the lot at Lordstown. The employee lot. He wanted to see if the lights were on.”

s05a.slug: TUESDAY · 2:06 AM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, THE LANDING WINDOW
body: The landing window is open its six inches. Below it one sodium lamp lights the Lagoon path orange, the light lying along the asphalt in a single long smear, and nothing on the path moves.
Jack sits on the sill with his back against the frame and the phone shut in his hand. In Youngstown it’s after five in the morning, and he doesn’t know which room his father is asleep in.

The pack of Reds is in the Carhartt’s inside pocket, where it lives. He takes it out and holds it on his knee, the cellophane catching the orange. Four left. He turns it end over end, once, and decides nothing about it at all.
Past the path the eucalyptus stand in the orange light without a leaf moving.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 3:40 PM · MISSION STREET POST OFFICE
body: The Mission Street post office has one window open and a line to the door, and the radio behind the counter is playing this morning’s memorial from Fort Hood over again, low — a bugle, then the President. Nobody in line talks.

Jack waits with the reader in his bag and, in his front pocket, the fold of tip money he’s been keeping back for Friday. At the window he asks for a money order, twenty dollars, and fills in PAY TO from memory — D. KOSTELNIK, STRUTHERS, OH — and leaves FROM blank. Twenty-one ten with the fee. He counts it out of the fold: singles, a five gone limp, a dime. The clerk tears off the customer’s receipt and slides it across, and Jack drops the envelope in the slot marked OUT OF TOWN.
Outside, Rafi Ochoa is sitting on the curb with his skateboard rocking under one heel and a flat-rate box on his knees, addressed in fat felt-pen capitals to OXNARD.
“Boss.” He lifts the box. “My other abuela. My mom’s mom. She gets a box when the first one gets a box. It’s a cold war. I’m just the mailman.”
His eyes touch the receipt in Jack’s hand and go back to the street. “No stress, boss,” he says, though Jack hasn’t said anything.

Then: “I saw Priya get you at the front desk yesterday. With the pink.” A shrug. “Pink’s money. Everybody knows pink.” The board rolls forward and back under his heel. “You need work? I got an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.”
Jack looks at him.

“Vitamins, boss.” Rafi shows both palms, the box balanced on his knees. “Not bars. I don’t do bars.” He holds out a hand for something to write on, and the only paper Jack has is the receipt. Rafi turns it over on his thigh and writes his number on the back in ballpoint, ten digits with a little wave drawn under them, and hands it back.
“Marcus Aurelius says what stands in the way becomes the way,” he says, getting up. “Pretty sure he meant rent.”
He tucks the box under his arm and carries it inside to stand in the line. Jack puts the receipt in his wallet behind the Mooney ID, with the other two.

journal.title: Rafi Ochoa (204)
journal.text: Rafi Ochoa. Second floor. Carried my fridge up four flights and was gone before Dad could tip him. Calls everybody boss. Lent me his bike on the wharf at one in the morning like it was nothing, till Christmas. His father’s a detective. He sells weed, and Adderall around midterms. Not bars, he says. Outside the post office he offered me an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 5:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE NEWMAN LOUNGE
body: At half past five the Newman lounge is lit by two lamps and the Coke machine, and through the window the olive in the courtyard has gone black against the last green of the sky. Somebody has left a guitar on the couch, and a Bible study’s worth of Styrofoam cups.

The box is on the coffee table — Priority Mail, COEUR D’ALENE ID in the postmark, taped on every seam twice. Becca is kneeling beside it with Mrs. Fitch’s good scissors, which Mrs. Fitch lent her personally, and she has plainly been waiting; there is an order to this, and the order is that he watches.

She opens it. On top is a letter on the cow stationery, Holsteins grazing up the margins, in Mrs. Lindell’s upright hand, and Becca reads it to him. *Dear Jack, Becca tells me you are her boyfriend now, which we knew. Please find enclosed.* There’s a good deal after that about the weather in Rathdrum and a heifer with opinions, and the word *boyfriend* comes up twice more, and each time Becca reads it a little faster.
Then a tin of molasses cookies with wax paper between the layers. Then a pair of gray wool socks so thick they stand up on their own.
“North Idaho socks,” Becca says.
“Becca. My feet are in *California*.”
“That’s what they’re for.”

At the bottom, wrapped in the *Coeur d’Alene Press*, two jars of huckleberry jam, purple-black, with masking-tape labels in her mother’s Sharpie. One says JACK. The other says FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE.
“Mom thinks everybody’s Catholic till proven otherwise,” Becca says.
“Theo’s been proven otherwise in several jurisdictions.”

The pink corner is showing out of the reader in his bag. Becca, making room for the jars, sees it and holds out her hand for it the way she’d hold it out for a permission slip, and he gives it to her. She reads it with her finger under the line, and her finger stops at HOLD.
“I have six hundred and twelve dollars,” she says. “From Daisy. She was a very good heifer.”

She sold Daisy at the Kootenai County Fair in August of last year and put it in the credit union in Coeur d’Alene and hasn’t touched it, because it was for something that mattered. She explains all of this with his envelope in her hand. There is nothing in her face but the offer.

choices.text: Take her hand. “Keep Daisy. I mean it.”
choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You took her hand and told her to keep Daisy.
response: He takes her hand across the box — marker on the knuckles, a nick healing on one of them — and says it. “Keep Daisy. I mean it.”
Becca looks down at their hands, and up at him, and nods once. “Okay,” she says, and keeps hold of him. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

In 412 that night Theo receives the second jar on his feet. He reads the label, holds the jar up to the desk lamp so the light comes through it purple, and inclines his head in the general direction of Idaho. “Tell Mrs. Lindell I’m a supporter, not a member.” He shelves it beside the espresso machine, label out, next to the jar from his birthday.

choices.text: “I can’t accept a cow. My mother would hear about it.”
choices.key: Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You told her you couldn’t accept a cow.
response: “I can’t accept a cow,” he says. “My mother would hear about it.”

Becca laughs, and then she gets serious about it, because she takes his mother seriously. “She’d be proud of you. Daisy was a good cow.” She folds the envelope along its crease and hands it back. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

response: “I can’t take your heifer, Becca.”

She hears it out and nods, weighing it on its merits. “Okay. That’s a real answer.” She folds the envelope along its crease and slides it back into the reader for him. “It’s there, though. Daisy doesn’t mind.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 9:40 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE DISH PIT
body: The Hobart runs its cycle with a long rising gargle and a thump, and under it Rudy’s transistor is on KNX, a man reading the traffic on the 405 to a kitchen a couple of hours north of it.

Jack racks coffee cups and tells Rudy about Rafi’s offer as a bit — one ride, two hundred dollars, Rafi’s abuela must run a very tight ship. Rudy doesn’t turn around from the flat-top. He works the scraper in long, even strokes toward the trough.
“I know what an errand is, mijo.”
Jack tries a second one, about Rafi’s abuela and the Marcus Aurelius, and Rudy lets it go by like the KNX weatherman. He doesn’t say anything else for the rest of the rack.

Gloria comes back from the walk-in with a crate of lemons on her hip, sets it on the steel, and counts the tip jar at the pass into little towers of quarters. The reader is on the shelf over the dish station where Jack’s bag lives, the pink corner sticking out of it. Gloria reaches up without asking, tugs the corner out far enough to read the number, and tucks it back.
“I can front you against December, hon,” she says to the quarters. “Don’t tell Rudy. He’ll want one.”
“No, Gloria. Thank you.”
She looks at him over her glasses. Then she sweeps the towers into an envelope and lets him.
At two minutes past ten the RAZR goes off in his apron, and goes off again, and keeps going.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 11:20 AM · THE BENCH ABOVE CAMPUS POINT
body: Veterans Day, and the feast of St. Martin of Tours; half the campus is closed for the first and has never heard of the second. The day is clear and mild and much too big. The Channel lies flat blue out to the islands, and below the bluff the kelp sits on the water in dark rafts, barely moving. Down by the Marine Lab a man in a VFW cap stands at the foot of the flagpole with a thermos, at attention, for reasons of his own. Jack has slept three hours in two nights, and it shows up as light: everything is too bright, the edges of things a little sharp, the gulls too loud. He has the reader on his knees, the pink envelope still folded in it at Hume, at the part about miracles. He hasn’t told anybody out here about one o’clock Tuesday morning. Theo lifted his head off the pillow when the phone went and put it back down, and hasn’t said a word about it since, and that is Theo’s kind of mercy.
Lena comes along the bluff path with her bag on one shoulder and two oranges in her cardigan pockets, and sits down on the bench, and studies him.

body.text: “You look like a man who argued with a whiteboard and won,” she says. “It’s worse.”
body.else: “You look like a man who argued with a whiteboard and lost,” she says.

body: His hand has the Reds out of the Carhartt and one shaken loose more or less on its own. Lena holds out her palm.
He puts the cigarette in it. She takes the worship aid for the 12:10 out of her bag, turns it over, and writes on the back with the pen from her cardigan pocket:

body.title: The back of the 12:10 worship aid
body.text: No. 9 · Campus Point · 11/11/09 · Veterans Day

body: She rolls the cigarette up in it and puts it in the tin with the other eight. Then she checks her watch — eleven twenty-four, enough time before the Communion fast — and starts on an orange, getting the peel off in one long curl with her thumbnail.

“Martin of Tours,” she says. “Roman cavalry. A beggar at the gate in Amiens in the dead of winter, and Martin takes his sword and cuts his own cloak down the middle and hands him half.” She splits the orange and gives Jack the bigger piece without looking to see which it is. “Everybody forgets the beggar took it. That’s the half nobody puts on the holy card.”
“Patron saint of?”
“Soldiers. Beggars. Innkeepers. Geese.” She ticks them off on orange-sticky fingers. “When they came to make him a bishop he hid in a barn full of geese, and the geese honked till they found him.”
“So the geese ratted him out,” Jack says, “and got a feast day.”
“They got *eaten* on his feast day. That’s different.” She licks her thumb. “That’s Europe for you.”
She eats her half a section at a time and watches the islands and leaves him all the room he wants to say it in.

choices.key: On the bench above Campus Point you told Lena about your father’s night in the Lordstown lot.
response: So he tells her. The RAZR on the desk at two minutes past one; his mother very calm; the bar on Midlothian and the Steelers game, his father who spits at the Steelers; Nonna’s beads on the oilcloth; the garbage can going over at the curb at ten to five, which he heard down the phone. The employee lot at Lordstown, to see if the lights were on. He tells it badly and out of order, and she doesn’t fix the order.
She doesn’t argue, either, and she doesn’t tell him it’s going to be fine. When he runs out she looks at the water.

“Daddy didn’t drink,” she says. “After the storm. He gutted houses. Ours first, then Grandmère’s, then anybody’s on Banks Street who’d let him in the door with a crowbar. All that winter Mama would find him asleep in the truck in front of somebody else’s house with the sheetrock dust still in his hair.” She turns a strip of peel over in her fingers. “Some men drink and some men gut houses. Yours hasn’t got a house to gut, Jack.”
He doesn’t have an answer to that.
“Call him Saturday,” she says. “Ohio State’s playing Iowa. Don’t talk about it. Talk about that.” And then, unprompted:

response.text: “And I’m glad you said it, Monday. About him.”
response.else: “What I said Monday — I’d have said it different if I’d known.”

response: Since he’s telling things, he tells her the rest: the pink envelope folded in the reader, three hundred and forty dollars by Friday at five. She reads it and hands it back.

response.text: “I’ve got forty dollars,” Lena says, “and a court-bouillon.”

response: Jack laughs for the first time since Monday.

He opens the RAZR to Tuesday night and hands it over. Lena reads Gina’s thread as if it were her own phone: thumb on the arrow, one text at a time, her mouth moving a little at *mrs d gave me detention*.

“Tell her the truth about that girl’s daddy isn’t hers to use,” Lena says. “A thing can be true and still not be yours to spend.” She thumbs down. “And tell her I’d have said it too. At fifteen I’d have said it *louder*. Sister Mary Margaret had to separate me from a girl named Courtney Dugas over the Louisiana Purchase. I was *right*, Jack. It didn’t help.”

She gets to the last one. *dad drove home like that monday. i heard the truck hit the can.* He watches her read it. She stays on it a little while. She closes the phone with a click and gives it back, and for a second her hand rests on the back of his on the bench, and then she goes back to her orange.
“How are you,” he says. “Actually.”

She has to know he’s changing the subject; she lets him, and answers anyway. Wes: nine days. She hasn’t heard from him and didn’t expect to. At four minutes past eight every night she still ends up on the east stairs with the LG shut in her lap, sitting through the minute it used to ring. “I’m going to stop,” she says. “Maybe Thursday.” She makes a face at the water. “Laney says it’s like a dog waiting at the door for a man who moved to Baton Rouge. Laney says a lot of things. She’s right about forty percent of the time. That’s a terrible percentage to live with.”

response.text: “Mémère called again Sunday night.” Lena tucks her feet up under her on the bench. “She says you have manners. She wants it noted.”

response: She folds the orange peel into a small square packet. “You’re still coming Thursday?”
“I promised.”
“He’ll like that.” She puts the packet in her pocket. “He thinks everybody leaves.”

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 1:10 AM · THE ANCHOR, UNDER THE HOBART
body: He worked Hector’s Wednesday so Hector could work his Thursday; it’s the first thing Thursday has cost him.

Ten past one on Thursday morning and the Anchor’s kitchen is down to the hum of the walk-in and Rudy scraping the flat-top for the last time tonight. Jack is on his knees on the rubber mat with his arm under the Hobart to the shoulder.
The Folgers can comes out with a skin of grease-dust on the lid. He counts it once, on the mat, in the light from the pass.

body.text: One hundred fifty-four dollars. The ANCHOR envelope is in a St. Vincent de Paul basket, and that’s where it should be.

He takes out his wallet. Behind the Mooney ID, three stubs, and on the back of the newest, Rafi’s number with its little wave. On the fourth floor of Delgado, Theo will be awake; Theo is always awake. Across the Commons the Brick’s circulation desk is short two people, and Priya will be behind it.
The kitchen smells of bleach water and the last of the bacon. The walk-in hums. Rudy scrapes. Rudy did six years at Soledad; Jack figures he has seen men count money on a floor before.

response: Rafi picks up on the second ring with the sea somewhere behind him. “Thursday, boss. Two o’clock, behind Delgado. Bring La Flaca.” At the flat-top, Rudy’s scraper stops, and then starts again.

body: The harbor at a quarter past two is hard white glare off flat water, and on the bait-dock float the sea lions are asleep in a heap, one of them complaining in its sleep.

The Vans shoebox rides in La Flaca’s basket, taped shut along every edge with blue painter’s tape. It is heavier than shoes. Rafi set it in the basket behind Delgado at two o’clock and said, “Back door of the Wharf Rat. Knock twice. Don’t open it, boss. It’s not your birthday.” Jack coasts down Mission with the coaster brake ticking and the box jumping at every seam in the road.
Ray Ochoa comes out of the Anchor as he’s passing it, a coffee to go in one hand and his windbreaker over the other arm, and Jack has to stop for him or hit him.
“Saint Isidore.” Ray’s eyes go to the basket and come back up. “New shoes?”
“My roommate’s.”

“Big feet, your roommate.” Ray blows across the lid of his coffee and looks out at the sea lions for a while. Then he walks off up the wharf toward Anacapa Street, toward the station, with his coffee.

The Wharf Rat’s back door is in the alley behind the bait shop, propped open on a mop bucket. Jack knocks twice on the frame. A man in a Raiders cap takes the shoebox, weighs it in his hands without looking at it, and gives him back two hundred dollars in twenties, folded once. “Rafi says gracias.” The door swings to against the bucket.

At 3:55, cutting Evan’s section to do it, at the Residential Services window, Jack puts two kinds of money on the counter: a hundred and forty out of the Folgers can, in fives and singles that smell like coffee, and Rafi’s twenties, crisp, smelling of nothing. The clerk counts them twice and types, and somewhere in the system a hold lets go.

journal.title: Ray Ochoa (Marisol PD)
journal.text: Detective Sergeant, per the badge wallet. Rafi’s father. Gray Crown Vic, a windbreaker, the Vehicle Code by heart. Knows my face from the Anchor counter: Tuesdays, meatloaf, a nod to Rudy. Did the bit: ‘License and registration.’ Asked what was in the bag and took ‘vitamins’ for an answer. Gave me a light out of his trunk. Found property. Thursday on the wharf: ‘Saint Isidore. New shoes?’ He didn’t look in the box.

s11b.slug: THURSDAY · 9:05 AM · RESIDENTIAL SERVICES, THE WINDOW
body: Residential Services opens at nine, and at five past Theo Vance is at the window in a navy blazer. On Theo, a blazer at nine in the morning means an event.
“Poppy has a recital,” he says. “La Cañada. I’m expected in the front row by two.”
The clerk wears her reading glasses on a beaded chain, and when Theo hands over his card she holds it up to the fluorescent light, and turns it over, and holds it up again.
“It’s real,” Theo tells her. “It’s just very ugly.”
She runs it. She looks at the slip, then at Theo, then at the blazer, and seems to reach some private conclusion about the state of higher education.
Jack is beside him with his wallet half out and his argument ready.
“It’s not charity, Costigan,” Theo says, signing. “It’s an investment in my roommate situation. I’ve seen the alternatives. One of them has a ferret.”
“It goes on the tab.”
“There is no tab.”
“There’s a tab, Theo.”
Theo takes the receipt from the clerk, turns it over on the counter, and writes on the back in small square capitals, holding the ballpoint like a fountain pen:

body.title: RESIDENTIAL SERVICES — RECEIPT (REVERSE)
body.text:
$340.00
+ 1 PIE (PEACH)
—T.A.V.

body: He hands it over. “The pie is non-negotiable. It’s how I’ll know you’re sincere.”

Jack puts the wallet back in his pocket. He knows what this is. Somebody is helping him, and his part is to stand still for it, and he would honestly rather do the Stations of the Cross on his knees up the Delgado stairs.
Theo is already at the door, checking the Submariner. “Peach, Costigan. Not a cobbler. A pie.”

“Hardship extension,” she says. “Per Section 4.2. I filled it out.”

She has: his name, his student ID, his room, and the rest in her smallest print. The one blank she’s left him is his mother’s maiden name, for reasons the form does not explain. He fills it in: RINALDI.

AMOUNT: $340.00 · CURRENT DUE DATE: 11/13/09
REQUESTED DUE DATE: 12/01/09, pending campus payroll (Pacifica Library, Circulation, night)

body: “How did you document it?”
“You texted me at the circulation desk at one in the morning, Jack. That’s documentation.”

The clerk reads it, and stamps it, and the hold slides to December first, pending payroll. The night desk at the Brick is tonight and Friday, midnight to six, eight-forty an hour; Priya has put him on the schedule already, in pencil. “Eight shifts, after withholding,” she says. “I did the math. Two of them are this week.”

“I’ll want the sleeve back,” she says. “The sleeves are mine. I buy them by the hundred at the Staples on Mission, and Housing has not reimbursed me one time, and I’ve stopped asking, because asking would mean filling out a form, and I won’t be made to fill out a form to get reimbursed for the sleeves I put forms in.”
Jack thinks about that, and decides it’s airtight.
“Priya. Thank you.”

“It’s a form.” She looks at the stamp, not at him. “Forms are how people help each other without anybody having to look at anybody.” Then she does look at him, over the clipboard. “Don’t make me regret informing you.”

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning, on her twenty-first birthday. Her mother’s text came in at the dryers. She didn’t answer it in front of me. Filled out my hardship form before I asked. Laminated. She wants the sleeve back.

s12.slug: THURSDAY · 8:10 PM · CAFÉ BASTILLE, MISSION STREET
body: The espresso machine at Bastille screams straight through every quiet song, and an open mic is mostly quiet songs. String lights looped along the beams; a chalkboard sign-up by the register in six colors of chalk; a house guitar with its pickup held on by electrical tape; a tip jar labeled STRINGS & RENT. The room is warm and loud with people who came to hear exactly one person each.

body.text: He came by himself, the way he said he would.

body: Laney has a two-top against the brick, and Lena has the other chair, and Jack drags a third over from a table of freshmen and sits on it backwards. Theo is in La Cañada for Poppy’s recital and the dinner after; at six he texted Jack a picture of his own blazer, no caption. Laney is scoring the open mic as a panel of judges, a napkin per contestant, in eyeliner pencil, and sliding each one across for Lena to countersign.

body.title: Napkin (fourth on the board)
body.text:
TALENT: a *harmonica*.
POISE: none.
EVENING WEAR: cargo shorts. The judges are concerned.

body: Before Julian there are eight others, and Laney scores every one. A Pi Lam girl does Regina Spektor and gets EVENING WEAR: *strong*. A grad student reads a poem about his ex-girlfriend’s cat. It is clearly a poem about his ex-girlfriend. “The judges,” Laney murmurs, “would like to speak to the cat.” Lena countersigns everything with a fleur-de-lis, and between acts she leans across the little table and asks Jack whether he’s eaten today, and when he says yes she says “What,” and he can’t think of anything, and she pushes the rest of her croissant at him.

At the next table Yusuf Noorzai has two friends from his dorm and a candle stuck in a blueberry scone, and one of the friends announces to the café that he is nineteen today and has never been sung to. Lena is on her feet with the match still burning, leading the café in “Happy Birthday” in a key of her own choosing; the espresso machine comes in on the high note. Yusuf endures it with his eyes shut. “This,” he tells his friends, “is a Catholic potluck in *café* form.”

Later, while Lena is at the counter for napkins, Yusuf leans back on two legs of his chair until he’s level with Jack. “I watched the memorial Tuesday,” he says. “All of it. Standing up.” He lets the chair down. “Don’t ask me why.”

Julian is ninth on the board, in green chalk. He sits on the stool in an old brown cardigan with the guitar across his knee and tunes for a long time without apologizing for it. Lena leans over to Jack. “He tunes like it’s a sacrament.” “He tunes like he’s stalling.” She looks back at the stage. “Same thing, sometimes.” Then Julian leans in to the mic.
“This one doesn’t have a second chorus,” he says. “People kept leaving in it, so I cut it.”
A few people laugh. Lena doesn’t. Laney turns her eyeliner pencil around and around in her fingers and leaves the napkin blank.
It’s short. It’s about a house, and a mother, and a bus, and it isn’t about anybody in this room. He sings it close to the mic and nearly without moving:
*My mother tunes her C string down a hair / so the house hums a little flat in the rain. / The 51B goes by at midnight, lit up and empty. / I know every stop by the sound of the brakes.*

The espresso machine leaves this one alone. Lena sits through every bar of it with her elbows on the table and her coffee going cold at her wrist, and she doesn’t reach for the cup. The string lights are in her hair. Jack, who promised, stays to the end, and for the last verse he isn’t watching Julian.
When it’s over people clap the way they clap for a short song, surprised. Laney writes TALENT: yes. on a fresh napkin and folds it in half.
Julian comes back through the tables with the case in his hand, and he comes to Jack first.
“You stayed.”
“I said I would.”

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask.

response: “It was good,” Jack says.
“It was short.”
“That’s what I meant.”
Julian smiles down at the floor and turns to Lena, who has finally picked up her cold coffee.
“You really cut it,” Jack says.
“Took a hacksaw to it.” Julian shifts the guitar case to his other hand and weighs it. “It’s lighter. A second chorus is a repeat sign. Nobody wanted to go back.”
“She stayed too,” Jack says.
Julian looks at him, not at Lena. “I saw,” he says, and leaves it there.

s13.slug: THURSDAY · 10:32 PM · MISSION STREET → THE 11 BUS → THE LAGOON
body: On the sidewalk outside Bastille the string lights are still on and the chalkboard has been turned to face the wall. Julian comes out last with his guitar case, and stops beside Lena, and asks it gently, as if he were asking permission for something much smaller. “Can I walk you back?”
“Yes,” Lena says.
“Lovely set, Julian,” says Laney, perfectly polite. Her pink BlackBerry is in her hand, and it stays dark.

The 11 comes up Mission at twenty to eleven, nearly empty. Jack and Laney take the long back seat. Lena and Julian sit three rows up, a guitar case’s width between them, the case standing upright in the aisle with his hand on its neck. Laney rides down Ocean Road with her chin on the seatback in front of her and her eyes on the backs of their heads.

At the Anacapa stop Lena and Julian get off first. Laney waits on the curb until they’re up the path, and across the black water the door of Delgado opens its rectangle of light with two shapes standing in it, and then the light narrows to a line, and the line goes out. Then she hooks her arm through Jack’s and steers him the other way, round the far side of the Lagoon, into the dark along the water.
“Walk me home, fireman,” she says. “Apparently I’m available.”

choices.text: Give her your arm like an escort in the evening-gown round.
response: Jack crooks his elbow properly and walks her round the Lagoon at pageant pace, announcing her to the sleeping ducks: Miss Dallas County, her talent the baton, her platform literacy.

“And revenge,” Laney says. “Put revenge on the card.” She laughs, and the heels go on clicking, and she lets him do the question-and-answer round for her, world peace and all, the rest of the way round the water.

body: After the 12:10 the Grove is all light in strips: the sun coming down through the eucalyptus in long slats, the bark hanging off the trunks in curls like old wallpaper, the path under their feet loud with dropped leaves and the little gray-blue seed buttons that roll when you step on them. It’s Friday the thirteenth. At the first big trunk Lena stops, knocks on it twice with her knuckles, crosses herself, and catches him watching.

“Both,” she says. “I’m from New Orleans. We don’t insult either side.” And then, because she can’t help it: “Philip the Fair arrested the Templars on a Friday the thirteenth. 1307. That’s *French history*, Youngstown.” “With you everything is French history.” “Everything *is* French history. Y’all just don’t admit it in Ohio.”

body.text: He’s on five hours from the night desk, and the light comes through the trees at him like it’s personal.

body: She walks with her head tipped back, looking up into the canopy for the first clusters. It’s early yet, she says, but they’re coming; there’s a grove down the coast where they hang so thick by Christmas that the branches bend, orange and black folded up into gray so you’d take them for dead leaves. “And here’s the thing, Jack. They come back to the same trees every winter — the *same trees* — and not one of them has ever been here before. It’s four generations later. The ones that left in March are dead. These are their great-great-grandbabies. They just *know*.”
“That’s instinct,” Jack says. “Aquinas would call it the natural appetite of the thing. A butterfly can’t help it.”
“Aquinas would’ve put a monarch on a holy card if he’d ever seen one.”
“‘Another will gird you and carry you where you do not want to go,’” Jack says. “John 21. That’s grace. Ask Peter.”

“Grace,” Lena says, “is when you go somewhere you’ve never been and it turns out to be home.” She pokes him in the arm without looking down. “That’s Augustine with the cough taken out. You’re welcome.”

“Also they’re poison,” she adds, pleased about it. “They eat milkweed when they’re babies and they taste terrible forever after, and every bird on the coast learns it the hard way. Gorgeous and poison. Laney says it’s a business model.”

“They should try Ohio,” Jack says. “Everybody who ever left Youngstown comes back four generations later and can’t tell you why either. My cousin Vinnie came back from Phoenix. We still don’t know what for. The man had a pool.”

Then she stops dead on the path and takes a fistful of his sleeve. “*There*. Jack. Look.” On a low branch over the path, alone, a single monarch is opening and shutting its wings in a slat of sun, slow as breathing, orange going to gray and back. The first one. They stand under it without a word until it folds up and becomes a leaf again, and she lets go of his sleeve.

She laughs at the two of them, standing there, and it goes up into the trees. He keeps her going — the monarch as the patron saint of people who move back in with their parents; the monarch as the only creature on earth that has ever gone to Ohio on purpose — and she keeps laughing, and the light keeps coming down in strips across the cardigan, and for a stretch of a few hundred yards it’s as good a walk as he’s ever had with anybody.

“They cluster for warmth,” she says, eyes up in the leaves, “and they hardly feed all winter, they just hang on what they came with. Oh — Julian asked me to dinner, so. And when it warms up in February they all let go at once, and the air’s just full of them —”
She’s still talking about February. Jack catches her eyes on him, at the edge of his vision, and then on the trees again.

The rest of it comes the way facts arrive with her, whether he asks or not. Saturday. Somewhere with tablecloths; she’s going to have to iron something. “He asked if he could ask me something first,” she says, to a branch. “Then he asked.”
All Souls was eleven days ago. Jack does the sum without meaning to and gets it right.
A step later her eyes are on him again, and then up.
Jack smiles.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So.

She’s still laughing a step later, and it’s then that it arrives. Not a thought, nothing he could put into a sentence. Just a shape under his breastbone, the shape of the word *wait*, with nothing left inside it.
The thing he was going to ask her on Sunday goes back to wherever it has been all week.

s15.slug: FRIDAY · 4:35 PM · THE LIGHTHOUSE, THE BACK PORCH
body: The sun is ten minutes off the Channel, and the Lighthouse’s back porch has turned the color of a peach crate. A laptop in the kitchen window plays something slow that sounds recorded underwater. The surfers who rent the place have a keg in a trash can of ice by the steps, FRIDAY THE 13TH on the lid in Sharpie and a horseshoe hung on the tap.

Theo got back from La Cañada at three and stood in the doorway of 412 in the blazer until Jack got up. “Come drink something with a label, Costigan.” Now he’s leaning on a porch post with a Stella, and Jack is working the porch.

He has three surfers with their wetsuits peeled to the waist and a girl in a Marisol Crew sweatshirt, and he’s giving them Friday the thirteenth as a feast of the Church: Philip the Fair arrested every Templar in France on a Friday the thirteenth, 1307 — so it’s a solemnity in Paris and a holy day of obligation for anybody with a castle. The keg, he tells them, is a sacramental. Not a sacrament — it can’t confer grace on its own; it depends entirely on the disposition of the recipient — and he raises a red Solo cup to it, a toast and not a blessing, since he isn’t ordained and the keg isn’t Catholic, and they cheer. Then the Youngstown liturgical year, on his fingers: Advent; Christmas; the feast of the first pothole; Lent; the octave of the Browns’ elimination; Ordinary Time, which is summer (a Tuesday); and the opening of deer season, a solemnity. The surfers love Youngstown. One of them wants to go.
Theo, from the post, not loud: “That’s three bits in a row. You don’t do three.”

Jack does a fourth. The surfer with the St. Christopher on a bootlace, it turns out, is wearing a saint the Vatican took off the calendar in 1969. That makes him the only man on this porch surfing uninsured. The porch laughs. Theo looks at Jack over the neck of the Stella, and lets him have it, and takes the Stella into the house.

When the laugh is done Jack is looking west, past the gap in the back fence, out to the Point. The light out there has gone the color of weak tea. Below the dead lighthouse, small, at the low stone wall by the white cross, a man sits with a guitar case open on the stones beside him. Jack knows the shoulders from a stool at Bastille. Julian is playing to nobody, and the wind brings none of it this far.

The screen door bangs. Theo comes out with two Coronas, a lime wedged in each neck, and stops beside him at the rail and sees where Jack is looking. He puts one of the bottles in Jack’s hand. Then he goes back inside, and he does not look west.

The bottle is so cold it aches in his palm. Jack holds it until the sun is gone, and then he sets it on the rail and walks home across the Grove with the eucalyptus black overhead and his hands in the pockets of the Carhartt.

By ten the fourth-floor lounge has been annexed by organic chemistry. Three Bio 1A pre-meds have the big table under a drift of Priya’s old flashcards, laminated in 2007 and handed down like a family Bible, and Kevin, in a gray quarter-zip, stands at the half of the whiteboard Margot’s verdict isn’t on, drawing an enolate for the fourth time. Doug is asleep on the couch under a fleece blanket with a wizard on it. Jack has the other end of the couch and the reader.

He’s been doing the reagents. LDA is St. Jerome: bulky, bad-tempered, won’t attack anybody, just walks in and takes the least-crowded proton out of spite. Grignards are Jesuits — brilliant, they’ll react with absolutely anything, and one drop of water ruins them. The pre-meds have been writing it on Priya’s flashcards in Sharpie. One of them, a sunburned kid from Visalia named Garrett, has laughed loudest at every one of them and slapped the table.

It’s Garrett who brings up Maine. He says it capping a highlighter, conversational, as if it were the weather. “I don’t know, I think Maine got it right. Marriage is for kids. That’s what it’s *for*.” The girl beside him nods at her flashcard.
Kevin caps the marker and turns around. “Biology doesn’t vote, Garrett,” he says, each word set down separately, like instruments on a tray. “People do.” He puts the marker on the ledge.
The table goes quiet. Garrett laughs once, waiting for the rest of the joke, and when there isn’t any rest his ears go red and he looks down at his flashcard.

Then Kevin’s smile comes back, all its team-captain wattage, half a second late and on crooked, like a picture hung in a hurry. “Getting water,” he says. “Carbonyls. Don’t touch my enolate.” Through the wall Jack hears the stairwell door.

response: Jack leaves Hale open on the arm of the couch and goes out after him.

Jack turns the room. It isn’t hard. He does himself as a Grignard reagent — eager, reacts with everything, undone by the first drop of water — and Garrett, still pink, says that’s every freshman on the fourth floor, and gets his laugh, and by twenty to eleven he has the table back on carbonyls, St. Jerome and all. Kevin’s chair stays pushed out from the table, the marker on the ledge where he left it.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water.

s16a.slug: FRIDAY · 10:22 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, BETWEEN FOUR AND FIVE
body: The east stairwell is painted cinderblock and caged bulbs and ten degrees colder than the hall. Jack is halfway up the flight between four and five when he hears them, a landing above, at the top, where the roof door says ALARM WILL SOUND and doesn’t mean it.
Kevin’s voice, low and fast, nothing sunny in it. “You said you’d never —”
And Theo’s, lower. “I haven’t.”

Jack’s sneaker squeaks on the tread. Above him both of them look down over the rail: Kevin with one hand on the push bar of the roof door; Theo on the top step with his knees up and his iPhone dark in his hands.
“Costigan!” Theo says. “We were discussing Doug’s raid schedule. He’s a Tauren druid. It’s a lifestyle.”

Kevin comes down the stairs. On the way past he puts a hand on Jack’s shoulder for one step — warm through the flannel, there and gone — and goes on down to four, to the lounge and the enolate and Garrett.
Theo doesn’t get up. He waits, friendly, for Jack to go back down.

s16b.slug: FRIDAY · 11:05 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: At five past eleven Jack sits on the third step up from the fourth-floor landing, where the one bar lives, and calls Glenwood Avenue.

It rings in the kitchen in Youngstown, where it’s after two in the morning — six times, eight — and goes to the machine: his mother’s voice, recorded the year Rosie was born, asking him to leave a message for the Costigans, God bless. He hangs up before the beep. The house is asleep. There’s no one at the table with a rosary, waiting on a truck. He sits there with the phone shut in his hand and lets himself have that.
From above him, up past five, by the roof door, Kevin’s voice comes down the stairwell, low and fast. “You said you’d never —”
And Theo’s, lower. “I haven’t.”
Somebody opens the roof door on the night and lets it shut again. The alarm doesn’t sound; it never has. Jack looks up the well of the stairs at the caged bulb on five, and doesn’t go up.
