body: On the lounge TV it’s the fourth quarter in Columbus under a sky the color of dishwater, the Horseshoe full to the rim and breathing steam, and in the lounge the blinds are half down against a California afternoon that doesn’t know what month it is.

Becca is on the carpet in front of the set, cross-legged, in his gray Cardinal Mooney hoodie with the sleeves rolled three times, explaining downs to a room that didn’t ask. Theo is on the arm of the couch with a Pellegrino. Laney has her bare feet on the coffee table, ankles crossed. Margot is in the armchair with a library Bourdieu open on her knee; she is here, she has said, to observe a ritual. Down the hall Kevin’s door has been shut since last night.

body.text: Jack has slept four hours since the night desk, from half past six to half past ten.

body: Jack is calling the game from the couch, play by play. Pryor keeps it on third and long and goes left, all legs, six foot six of Jeannette, P-A — “the only man in Ohio who runs like he’s late for Mass.” Tressel on the sideline in the sweater vest: “That vest has been to more funeral luncheons than my nonna. That vest has opinions about the ham.” And his father’s theory, delivered as settled doctrine: the forward pass is a Protestant innovation, legal since 1906, and Notre Dame only went and perfected it to save it from them. Becca laughs at all of it with her head back against his shin, and corrects him on the downs. Laney, with her eyes shut: “Deductions for excessive personality.” “He gets *extra* for personality,” Becca tells her.

At the TV timeout she gets up on her knees and pulls a flat package out from under the couch, where she has apparently been hiding it since before he got here. It’s wrapped in a Walgreens bag slit open and turned inside out, taped at every seam. “Okay,” she says. “Open it.”

body.text: It’s the two of them at Piedras Blancas at sunset, printed at the Walgreens on Mission, taken at arm’s length by Becca, who has cut off the top of her own head and kept all of his, with the elephant seals heaped on the sand behind them like a delivery of sofas.
body.else: It’s the two of them on the bleachers at the Friday-night game, printed at the Walgreens on Mission, taken by a dad in the row behind with Becca’s camera, his thumb a pink blur in one corner.

body: The frame is from the Goodwill, and she has painted it herself: elephant seals all the way around the border, gray and fat and very carefully done, and under each one, in tiny white capitals, what it weighs. 4,500 LBS. 1,600 LBS. 75 LBS (A PUP).
“For your desk,” Becca says. “Theo says you have no personal effects.”
“I said *affect*,” says Theo, from the arm of the couch.

Becca has plans. Gerald the turkey is thriving, which is the problem: her little brothers have taught him to come when he’s called, and her father says that’s the last thing a turkey ought to know. On Thanksgiving she’s going to call Jack at two o’clock her time, five in Ohio, during her dad’s grace — “so you can hear it. It’s eleven minutes. He does every cow.” She squeezes his arm and leaves the rest of Thanksgiving alone. “And next Saturday — The Game. Michigan. I looked it up.” It’s in her planner already, in green. “Can we watch it here? With you?”
Jack says they can watch it here.
Ohio State punts. Becca watches the ball go up and turn over at the top, and says, without looking away from it, “Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?”
Jack tells her it’s okay to say.

Iowa ties it with a freshman quarterback named Vandenberg who wasn’t supposed to be playing, and the game goes to overtime, and in overtime Iowa comes up empty. Then Tressel sends out Devin Barclay, a walk-on who used to play pro soccer, to kick a thirty-nine-yarder for the Rose Bowl. Becca gets up on her knees with her hands together and prays a Glory Be out loud at the TV. Laney says, “Amen.”
The ball goes through. Twenty-seven, twenty-four. Becca throws both arms up and hollers, and Theo applauds the television, and the announcers say *Pasadena* twice.

Margot turns a page. “That’s surface acting,” she says, not looking up. “Hochschild. *The Managed Heart*, 1983. Delta flight attendants, smiling through turbulence because the smile is the job.” She cites it like a bus schedule. “You were doing it last night. I was at the vending machine while you made three pre-meds laugh at carbonyls. Carbonyls aren’t funny, Costigan. I’ve checked.”
“He’s not acting,” Becca says. “He’s *happy*. They’re *winning*.”
Theo is already on his feet, pitching to the room at volume: “Terrelle Pryor. A small town in Pennsylvania. A mother who believed. Denzel as the coach — no. Denzel as the *vest*.”

response: Jack stands up with the frame against his heart. “I’d like to thank the Academy. And my father, who taught me the forward pass is Protestant. And Jim Tressel’s vest, which couldn’t be here today.” The lounge laughs; Becca claps with the Walgreens bag in her lap. Margot looks at him over the Bourdieu for a second, turns the page, and writes nothing down.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, and goes down the hall.
“Becca,” Jack says. “Explain downs to Margot.”

Becca turns round on the carpet to face the armchair and does, from first principles, with the coffee table for a field and Theo’s Pellegrino for the line to gain. Four tries to go ten yards; if you don’t, the other team gets it; you punt so they have farther to go. Margot closes the Bourdieu on her finger and listens to every word of it, to the end of fourth down.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, and goes down the hall.
“Leave it, Margot.”
She looks at him over the book, and leaves it. Becca, folding the Walgreens bag into a neat square to keep, doesn’t notice anything.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, and goes down the hall.
“Hochschild,” Jack says. “Page number?”
Margot looks up for the first time. “Chapter three,” she says, “and you’re welcome to it,” and goes back to Bourdieu, and Becca asks who Hochschild plays for.
On her way out Laney stops behind the couch and squeezes the back of his neck, once, hard, and goes down the hall.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants.

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH-FLOOR LANDING
body: The RAZR goes off in his pocket before he’s up off the lounge carpet, and the little outside screen says DAD.
His father hasn’t called him since September. Jack takes it out to the east stairwell, to the third step up, and sits.

body.text: He was going to call at the final. Lena told him to — talk about the game, not the other thing. His father has beaten him to it.

body: “Overtime,” says Frank Costigan. Behind him a space heater ticks and a radio is turned down low, and Jack could draw the garage from here: the Stroh’s fridge, the folding chair, the pegboard with the outlines of the tools on it.

response: “Rose Bowl, Dad.”

“Pasadena,” his father says, like it’s a town he means to drive to. And then four minutes of it: the walk-on kicker who used to play soccer for money (Frank has decided not to hold it against him); Pryor’s legs, and what Frank would do about Pryor’s arm; the freshman from Iowa who should’ve been scared and wasn’t; Tressel’s play-calling in the third quarter, a matter Frank intends to take up with God. Jack says *yeah* and *I know* and *he did*. Then: “Your mother says you needed money.”

s19.slug: SUNDAY · 12:50 AM · THE ANCHOR, THE END OF THE COUNTER
body: Ten to one and the end of the Saturday shift. The jukebox is dark, and the pie case is down to one wedge of lemon meringue sitting in its own light. Jack is on the last stool with his apron balled in his lap and his hands still pink from the sink.

body.text: Back in the kitchen, before he came out, Rudy watched him fold his tip-out into the Folgers can. The bills went in without a sound; there wasn’t much in there for them to land on. Rudy went back to wrapping the line and said nothing, for long enough that Jack heard it.

body: Gloria doesn’t come down the counter. She passes behind the server station with a bus tub on her hip, sets a coffee at his elbow across the gap without breaking stride, and keeps going to the urn, and with her back to him she asks, “How’s the pecan, hon?”
“She’s seeing somebody,” Jack says. “He’s nice.”
Gloria fills the urn to the line and screws the lid down. One breath.
“Lattice-top,” she says, and carries the bus tub through to Rudy.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top.

body: At a quarter past eleven Sully’s bell hangs quiet, its rope tied off to the cleat. The Saints are in a dome in St. Louis against a team with one win, and it’s closer than it has any business being. Dale is on his stool at the end of the bar in the Barry Sanders jersey. Lena has the chair under the bell in her black and gold, one boot hooked on the rung and one hand on the cleat, like she’s minding a horse.

Becca came straight from the six o’clock touch tank and has already done the cow holler twice, on a field goal and on a first down. “Hollering is not a talent, Miss Idaho,” Laney tells her after the second one. “The judges have discussed it.” Becca does it a third time, at her. Kevin drove; he sits at the end of the table, quiet, and watches the game like a chart. Theo came along in sunglasses to a sport he openly doesn’t follow and asks, at intervals, which ones are ours. At ten Laney ordered a mimosa on the strength of a Louisiana driver’s license that says she’s twenty-four and named Bernadette Thibodeaux.

body.text: Kevin saved Jack the seat beside him, and keeps passing him hot sauce he hasn’t asked for.

body: At the half Becca tows Jack to the Bloody Mary bar at the far end of the room for a virgin one, because of the celery. Up there the halftime show is a wall of noise — three men in suits shouting about tonight’s Colts game — and the table is a long way off. She leans in, practical and low. “Did you ask her yet?”

The second half kicks off before he can answer. Courtney Roby takes it at his own three and doesn’t stop, and the room comes up out of its chairs, and the line breaks, and Becca is swept off toward the table with both arms in the air, calling back over her shoulder, “I’m *praying*!”

Ninety-seven yards. The owner unties the rope, and Lena rings it for Roby standing up on the chair rung. Jack, back in the booth, gives the return a homily: a man with no kickoff touchdowns in his career, not one, and on the ninth Sunday the Lord says *go*. “It was Thomist, is what it was. He didn’t run toward the end zone. He ran away from everything that wasn’t the end zone.” Lena cracks up so hard she has to grab the rope to stay on the chair.

It’s a day when Brees throws two to the wrong team, and the Rams hang around. Then, early in the fourth, with the Rams within four, Brees finds Meachem from twenty-seven yards out, and the ball is in the air, and Sully’s is on its feet.

response: Jack is up on the booth seat before Meachem comes down with it. *WHO DAT* — from the bottom of a pair of Youngstown lungs — and Sully’s comes in under him, a hundred people in black and gold. Lena rings the bell for him, leaning back on the rope with all her weight, and when it’s over she reaches across and puts the end of it in his hand. It’s heavier than it looks, rough with a lot of Sundays, warm from her fist. Across the table Theo watches all of it with his arms folded.

It ends twenty-eight to twenty-three. Nine and oh. The owner unties the rope himself and rings it once more for the final. At Laney’s elbow the mimosa has gone warm and flat, the orange settled to the bottom.

Lena wipes the 8 off with her sleeve and holds out her hand to Kevin for the polish. “I’m not letting you near a nine,” she tells Jack, and does it herself, big and straight, and steps back to look.

s21.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Soon and Very Soon”
body: The nine o’clock is the candle Mass. St. Brendan’s is lit from the floor up — tapers on every sill under the blue glass, the sanctuary lamp, the votive rack at the shrine like a town seen from a hill at night — and over it the fir ribs go up into the dark like the hull of a boat somebody turned over and left. The student choir has two guitars and Kenzie Rourke on tambourine, and they take the processional at a clip, like they intend to have everybody before the King by ten.
Becca has saved three seats in the fourth pew on the left, her coat on one and her planner on the other. She moves the planner for Jack and leaves the coat. “For Lena,” she whispers.

body.text: She’s still a little hoarse from the WHO DAT, and proud of it.

body: Lena comes up the side aisle during the second verse with the black mantilla over her hair, and Julian Park-Ellis is a step behind her in a cardigan mended at both elbows. He isn’t carrying anything, and his right hand keeps closing on a guitar-case handle that isn’t there.

Becca lights up, and there’s nothing in it but welcome. “Oh! *Scoot*.” She scoots; Jack scoots; Lena slides in on his right with Julian on the aisle. Becca, Jack, Lena, Julian. “Julian,” Lena murmurs across him, and that’s the introduction. “She brought *somebody*,” Becca whispers into Jack’s shoulder, and squeezes his arm about it, and finds the page.

Julian sits through it like a man who never has, and it shows the way a new guy shows on a loading dock: he stands half a second after everybody and sits half a second after, and watches Lena’s hands to find out what to do with his. He doesn’t try the responses. He listens to them.

Father Osei reads the Gospel himself — the sun darkened, the stars falling out of the sky — and then, without changing his voice, the fig tree. *Learn a lesson from the fig tree. When its branch becomes tender and sprouts leaves, you know that summer is near.* On Jack’s right Lena stops moving. Not her hands, not her breath; the lace at her temple doesn’t stir.

body.text: Jack thinks of a shotgun house on Zimple Street he has never seen: For Sale since the storm, a fig in the side yard, and on the back porch, under the fig, a claw-foot tub.

body: The homily is short, even for Osei. “Heaven and earth will pass away,” he says, and waits out a cough in the back. “He doesn’t say *you* will. He says His words won’t.” He sits down, and the choir has to scramble.

At the consecration Jack kneels between Becca and Lena, a shoulder on either side of him, and for as long as the bells go he isn’t thinking about anybody at all. Julian kneels when the pew kneels and then stays down through the Our Father, alone on the kneeler with the church standing over him, until Lena touches his sleeve. At Communion he lets them by and sits back down by himself with his hands folded, and watches her go up.

In the crush at the doors afterward, with the choir still going, Jack hears him under his breath, humming the second Hosanna — the Holy, Holy he didn’t know an hour ago — and getting every note of it right.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end.

s22.slug: SUNDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD WALL
body: Afterward the courtyard is fifty-five degrees and perfectly still. The olive doesn’t stir. There’s no moon, and over the roof of the Newman house there are more stars than Marisol usually admits to, and low in the south one of them isn’t twinkling at all — just sitting there, brighter than everything else, steady as a porch light. Jupiter. Planets don’t twinkle. Jack learned that in the fourth grade and has been waiting nine years for it to come up.

Becca was across Ocean Road to the Ranger by two minutes past ten — the lab at eight. She hugged Jack hard, and then Lena, and then, after a second, Julian, who held still for it like he’d been warned and then hugged her back.

“I’ll get us coffees,” Julian says. He’s already turning toward the yellow door of the Newman house when he sees Jack on the wall, and the turn slows. “Take your time,” he tells Lena, and crosses the flagstones toward the light.
Lena sits up on the low wall with the mantilla folded in her lap and her boots hanging, and Jack sits beside her. It’s a week to the night. He said he’d ask, and he asks.
“So,” he says. “The table.”
He means the table, and only the table.

body.text: The joke he almost made on the walk to Lupe’s — *come to Youngstown, nobody there’s ever heard his name* — is still in his pocket, and it’s a different *his* now.

body: She answers like she’s had it ready; she’s had a week. “I’ll be okay at that table,” she says. “Wes will sit where he sits, and Josie will bite somebody, and Daddy will carve.” She breathes in through her nose and lets it go. “Julian says call him from the bathroom if I need to.”
It’s good advice. It’s exactly right, and Jack, who also had a week, didn’t think of it.
“You were nice about Friday,” Lena says.
“I’m nice.”
“You’re not, usually.” She knocks her boot heel against his. “That’s how I knew you meant it.”

Then she wants to hear about his, and he gives her the Greyhound like it’s a pilgrimage. Two and a half days. Changes in Denver and Chicago. He’s packing a rosary, a paperback and a sandwich he means to ration like the Donner Party, and by the law of averages he’ll be seated next to a man who sells knives out of a sample case and has a position on the moon landing. She’s still laughing at the knives when he gets to Nebraska, which he understands is four hundred miles of one cow standing in different places, and he does the cow. Lena says that in Louisiana that cow would be in a roux by North Platte.
“You’re going to come home a prophet,” she says, “or a serial killer.”
“In Youngstown they’ll want to know which before they set a place.”

Julian comes back across the flagstones with two coffees in Newman mugs, the white ones with the little leather boat on the side, and does the arithmetic — three people, two mugs — without breaking stride. He holds his out. “Jack. Take it. I’ll get another.”

response: Jack takes it. The mug is hot right through, too hot to hold properly, and he wraps his hands around it anyway and lets it burn a little.

Julian goes back in for another and comes out with it, and the three of them drink their coffee on the wall till the mugs are cold, talking about the fig tree and whether Osei times his homilies with a watch. Then they go out the gate to Ocean Road together, Julian on the street side.
“I’m good,” Jack says.

Julian doesn’t argue, and he doesn’t look put out. He sits down on Lena’s other side, and the two of them pass the one mug back and forth for the rest of it without either of them seeming to notice they’re doing it. When it’s empty the three of them go out the gate to Ocean Road together.
“You cut the second chorus,” Jack says, and leaves the mug where it is.

Julian glances past him at Lena on the wall, and something in his face goes very gentle. “Somebody had to stay to the end,” he says. He sits down on her other side and gives her hers and keeps his, and when the mugs are empty the three of them go out the gate to Ocean Road together.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday.

body: Monday Night Football with nothing riding on it sounds like a pool game nobody’s winning. Ravens at Browns is on one of the tube TVs in the corner with the volume down to a mutter, and the touchdown bell over the bar is tied off with a bar towel, the way Sully ties it on nights that haven’t earned it.
Dale has extended the Barry Sanders jersey to Mondays. Jack has a booth to himself and a Coke he’s been making last since kickoff.

Lena comes in at the end of the first quarter in the cardigan, with a root beer in each hand and a holy card pinched under one thumb against the bottle. She puts a root beer in front of him and slides in across the booth and props the card against the ketchup, facing the screen: St. Jude, green cloak, a little flame over his head.
“You watched mine win nine times, Youngstown,” she says. “I owe you a Monday.”

body.text: And then, under the TV, so only he gets it: “And it’s Monday.”

body: Dale cranes down the bar at the card. “That a saint?”
“St. Jude,” Lena says. “Hopeless cases. He’s for causes, Dale, not teams.”

“Young lady, the Lions have had that man on retainer since 1957.” He lifts his beer to the card anyway, and then, as one bereaved man to another, to Jack: “We get you people Sunday. Ford Field. Somebody’s gonna win a football game and it’s gonna be a tragedy either way.”

Jack does the first half as a wake. He gives Brady Quinn’s eulogy at the two-minute warning — a good son of Dublin, Ohio, a credit to Notre Dame, a man who threw the ball with real feeling in the general direction of other men — and he gives it again at the half, longer, because it’s nothing to nothing and the deceased has two quarters left. He does Eric Mangini’s press conference. He does the Dawg Pound as the Book of Lamentations. Lena answers with the 2005 Saints, who played their home games in San Antonio and Baton Rouge and went three and thirteen — the Babylonian Captivity, she calls it — and asks him who exactly he thinks he’s talking to about suffering.

The third quarter takes three minutes. The Ravens put up thirteen points in them, one of the touchdowns Dawan Landry going forty-eight yards the other way with a Quinn pass while the Browns offense watches him go like a bus they missed.
“St. Jude,” Lena says, squinting at the card, “has limits.”
It ends 16–0. Jack reads Quinn’s line off the screen in the voice his father uses for the obituaries: thirteen of thirty-one, ninety-nine yards, two interceptions.

choices.text: Pray to the card anyway. Out loud. For Brady Quinn’s soul.
response: Jack folds his hands over St. Jude and prays to him out loud, perfectly deadpan, at a volume that carries to the pool table: for Brady Quinn, who has suffered; for his offensive line, who were elsewhere; for the city of Cleveland, which has done nothing to deserve this except be Cleveland. Then, without changing his voice, and a good deal quieter, for a man watching this in a garage on Glenwood Avenue.

At the end of the bar Dale takes his cap off and holds it over the Barry Sanders jersey. Lena, who was laughing, stops at the last one, and puts her hand over his on top of the saint, and says the amen with him.

choices.text: “That’s not a lost cause. That’s a franchise.”
response: “That’s not a lost cause,” Jack says, nodding at the screen. “That’s a franchise.”

Lena lays St. Jude face down on the table, out of respect for the deceased. Dale says “*Hey*,” like he’s the one who’s been insulted, and then laughs into his beer, and the bartender comes down the bar to stand St. Jude back up against the ketchup himself.
“Thanks for coming,” Jack says.
Lena looks at him over the root beer. “I’m with Julian, Jack,” she says. “I’m not *dead*.” Then she steals a sip of his Coke and makes a face at how flat it’s gone.

s24a.slug: MONDAY · 8:40 PM · MISSION STREET, THE 11 BUS SHELTER
body: The shelter on Mission is a bench, a schedule last updated during the Clinton administration and a fluorescent tube that buzzes. Lena sits under it with Hale’s packet open on her knee, running a yellow highlighter down the margin.
The RAZR goes in his pocket. MOM. It’s twenty to twelve on Glenwood Avenue.
“Go,” Lena says, and turns a page.
He walks a block up Mission and round the corner past the laundromat, and stands with his back to the brick and the traffic between him and the shelter, and keeps his voice down anyway.
“*Zero!*” his mother says. “Did you *see*? *Zero.*”
He saw.
Then, with no breath in between, because she’s been sitting on it all game: “So? Christmas? Idaho?”
“Ma —”

“I wrote her already. Last week. On the good notepaper.” The good notepaper is the parish stationery with the crest, kept in the hutch for sympathy cards and First Communions. “A mother can write a girl. She wrote Rosie, didn’t she?”

body.text: “And Gina says the nun’s not coming.”

body: “She’s got a boyfriend, Ma.”
“*Again?*” His mother takes that in. “Madonna. Well. Idaho, then.”
There’s a click, and the hiss of the extension, and somebody breathing on the line. “Zero,” his father says. Click.

Jack listens for where. His mother is moving with the cordless — slippers on the linoleum, the back door — and then, faint and steady under her voice, the space heater in the garage, its fan rattling in its cage the way it has every winter of his life.
“He watched it home,” his mother says. “In the garage.”
Nonna’s asleep in the chair again, she says; still won’t do the stairs. Then she tells him to go to bed, it’s nearly midnight, and he doesn’t tell her it isn’t nearly midnight here.

When he comes back round the corner the 11 is pulling in, and Lena is up at the curb with the packet under her arm. She doesn’t ask. She gets on first and goes down the aisle and takes the aisle seat, and leaves him the window.

s25.slug: TUESDAY · 12:05 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Becca has been on the Portolá steps since five to twelve, in the sun, with two coffees in a cardboard tray, a maple bar on a napkin on her knee, and an envelope in her lap, address side down, that she is very visibly not looking at.

body.text: “I got your text,” she says, before hello, and hands him his coffee. “I’m so sorry about Thanksgiving. I mean I’m *happy* for Lena, I am, but you wanted to —” She stops, and draws a zipper across her lips, firmly. It isn’t hers to say. She tears the maple bar in half and gives him the bigger half. “Julian’s so *nice*,” she says instead. “Lena should date somebody nice.”

“Mrs. Fitch says Lena brought her young man to the nine o’clock!” Becca hands him his coffee. “I thought he was just *coming*. The way Theo comes to Sully’s. But Mrs. Fitch says he held her coat for her, and in 1962 that meant something.” She tears the maple bar in half. “Julian’s so *nice*. Lena should date somebody nice.” Then she stops, with her half in her hand, and he can watch her do it — the nine o’clock, the coat, *not yet* at eleven o’clock that night — adding it up. “You said not yet,” she says. There’s no edge on it anywhere. Then, before he can answer: “It’s okay. You don’t have to.” And she turns the envelope over in her lap.

body.text: …We would love to have you for a few days after Christmas, Rebecca, if your mother can spare you. Jack’s grandmother would like to meet the girl who writes on cows. With love, Maria Costigan

body: Her mother said yes before Becca finished the sentence; her father said “*Pittsburgh?*” the way he says *coyote*, and then yes. December twenty-seventh to the thirtieth. She has the flights printed already, Spokane to Pittsburgh through Denver — “it’s cheaper than Cleveland, I *looked*” — and the planner is open on the step beside her to a page headed OHIO!! with a list down it in green. ROSIE — crab book. NONNA — ??? GINA — ??? The crab book is half done, the pages tucked in the back of the planner: Thomas the hermit crab, drawn in marker, one page per true fact, the chip in his shell on every page so Rosie will know it’s him. “Is Youngstown a coat place or a coat-and-boots place? I have the boots. I have *so* many boots.”
“What does Nonna like? Is it bad I’ve never seen snow that wasn’t *ours*?” She looks at him with the whole sun on her face. “Jack. Your *house*.”

response: “They’ll love you,” Jack says, and it’s true.
Becca uncaps the green pen and writes, on her own, NONNA — ROSARY? and underlines the question mark twice.
Then she taps the letter twice against his chest, like a ticket being punched, and takes her coffee up the steps to her one o’clock with the planner under her arm.
“Let me talk to Ma.”
“Of course! She said you’d say that.” Becca finds the line for him, halfway down the first side, where his mother has written *He’ll want to talk to me first. Let him.* “See? She knows you.”
Then she taps the letter twice against his chest, like a ticket being punched, and takes her coffee up the steps to her one o’clock with the planner under her arm.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked.

s26.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE KITCHEN OFF THE FISHBOWL
body: At five past two in the morning the toaster in the kitchen off the Fishbowl is the only light on the ground floor of Delgado, the coils going orange through the slots. The Mr. Coffee has an inch of something black in it from Monday. The dented Newman stockpot Lena still hasn’t taken back is upside down in the dish rack. On the other side of the glass the Fishbowl is dark, the couches just shapes, and past it the sodium lamp makes an empty orange room out of the Anacapa lawn.

He got in from the Tuesday shift at twenty past one and didn’t go up. He’s making toast because his hands want something to do. The jar is on the counter by the toaster, purple-black, the lid labeled in a mother’s Sharpie: JACK.

body.text: It’s two in the morning. On the bleachers in September Becca said she’d pray for two in the morning, and Becca does what she says. Somewhere across the lawn, if he knows her at all, a girl with a rosary wound twice around her wrist has this exact hour in her hands, for him.
body.else: It’s two in the morning. Becca prays at two, like always. Somewhere across the lawn, if he knows her at all, a girl with a rosary wound twice around her wrist has this exact hour in her hands, for him.

body: The toast comes up. He spreads the jam with the back of a spoon, because the knives are all in the sink, and while he does it he walks her through the house. He can’t stop. He’s been doing it since noon yesterday.

She comes up the porch steps on Glenwood Avenue on the twenty-seventh of December in her Carhartt vest with a suitcase she packed a week early, and the porch is cold the way it’s always cold, and his mother has the door open before she’s up the steps. Rosie’s crab drawings are on the refrigerator under the St. Brigid’s magnet, and Becca can name every crab. Nonna sits her down at the kitchen table and wraps the beads around her hand and teaches her the Hail Mary in Calabrese, and Becca has it the first time, because Becca has everything the first time. His father is out in the garage, so Becca goes out to the garage, and by the second night his father likes her against his will and isn’t going to say so to anybody, ever. Gina rolls her eyes at her the first day and on the third day lets her braid her hair. And at dinner there’s the chair.

Becca would ask about the chair. She’d be gentle; she’s always gentle about a thing like that. His mother would tell her at the sink with her back turned, and Becca would put down the dish towel and take his mother’s hand. And from that night on, for the rest of her life — on the ranch, in a kitchen of her own someday with nine kids at the table and the beads worn smooth — Becca Lindell would pray for Danny Costigan by name. Every night. She wouldn’t miss one.

They’d love her. Every one of them would love her, and every one of them would believe it. His mother would stand at the stove and hope, right there in front of Nonna, in front of the chair, as hard as she knows how. And Jack would stand in his mother’s kitchen next to a girl he isn’t going to marry, and let her.
He puts the spoon down.

All fall there’s been a reason to wait, and the reason had a name. On Friday, under the eucalyptus, the name went to dinner with somebody else. He lifts the reason off, the way you’d lift your hand off a stack of papers by an open window to see what blows — and nothing moves. Not a sheet. He still can’t take Becca home.

A Hail Mary, and then her name, *Becca*, and then *Rebecca*, the way his mother wrote it on the good notepaper, and then just the name, over and over, at the minute she’s praying for him. He eats the toast cold, every bite, because her mother made the jam.
At two minutes past seven, from his bed, with Theo still asleep, he types it on the keypad a letter at a time and sends it.

s28.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:00 PM · PORTOLÁ LOT, THE RANGER
body: The Ranger’s heater ticks. With the doors shut it’s the only sound in the cab besides the engine turning over low under the floor — a small dry tick behind the dash every second or so, keeping time for somebody. Becca has had it running since before he came across the lot. It’s dark at six now. Portolá’s windows are lit in rows over the lot and the lot lights have come on orange over the cars, and none of it gets very far into the cab.

It’s Eli’s truck: the red ’94 with the Idaho plates and the Rathdrum Feed & Seed sticker peeling at one corner of the back glass, a bench seat with a Pendleton blanket over the split in the vinyl, St. Isidore clipped to the visor on her side with his plow. Two coffees in the cupholders, because she’s Becca and it’s six o’clock. His has a J on the lid in her marker. The planner is up on the dash, open to December. On the twenty-seventh, in pencil: PIT?
Her truck. Her heater, her keys, her saint. Whatever gets said in here, she can put it in drive whenever she’s ready, and nobody can make her wait. He’d have picked it himself if she hadn’t.
“They were out of the regular,” she says. “Yours is hazelnut. I’m sorry. I tasted it, it’s fine, it just tastes like a candle.”
He picks it up and holds it and doesn’t drink it. He has nothing funny in him tonight, and he doesn’t go looking.
She looks at his face once, in the orange from the lot. Then she reaches up and closes the planner before he’s said a word, and sets it on her knee with her hand on the cover.
“Is this a bad thing?”

Becca puts her hands on the wheel. She nods at the dark windshield, slowly — the nod she gives a weather report: no use arguing with it; you dress for it. “Okay,” she says. She keeps hold of the wheel.

Becca puts her hands on the wheel. “Try,” she says, as if she’s found it on the floor of the cab and is turning it over to see what it is. “You were *trying*?” He has nothing to put against it. She nods at the dark windshield, slowly — the nod she gives a weather report.

s28a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:14 PM · PORTOLÁ LOT, THE RANGER
body: Becca looks out at the lot. When she says it, it isn’t an accusation. She says it quietly, almost relieved to have it.
“You were going to bring *her*.”

She was praying Lena would say yes. She tells him that too. “I really was. Every night. I put it in with two in the morning.” She smooths the planner’s cover with her thumb. “I had it all worked out. She’d be at your mom’s and I’d be at ours, and I’d call during Dad’s grace, and you’d hold the phone out so everybody could hear him do the cows. I thought that was a good plan.” She says it like it was. It was.

body.text: “You said ‘not yet,’ Sunday.” She looks up at the visor. “I knew.”
“You told me Sunday it’s okay.” She picks her coffee up out of the cupholder and puts it back without drinking any. “It wasn’t, though.”

response: “Yes,” Jack says.
Becca nods. She takes it the way she took the first thing, all of it at once, without making him say any more. “Thank you,” she says, “for not saying no.”

response: “She’s with Julian,” Jack says. “And I still can’t take you.”
It takes her a second. He watches her get there: her eyes go down to the planner on her knee, and her mouth goes small. “Oh,” Becca says. “Oh, Jack. That’s worse. That’s so much worse for *you*.”
“This isn’t about Lena,” Jack says.
“Okay,” Becca says, and he can see that she believes him. She always has. She takes her hands off the wheel long enough to wipe her palms down her Wranglers, and puts them back.

s28b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:31 PM · PORTOLÁ LOT, THE RANGER
body: The heater ticks. Out in the lot somebody’s car chirps twice, locking, and a girl in a Portolá sweatshirt crosses behind the truck with a laundry basket on her hip.
Becca works it through where he can hear. “I did everything right. I know I did. It just isn’t the thing, is it.”
“You did,” Jack says. It’s the one thing in the cab he’s sure of. Past that he has no argument. There isn’t one; he’s looked.
“You looked at me like homework,” she says. “I thought if I was really good homework —” She stops.

Then she cries, with the engine running and her hands on the wheel, without making any noise at all. It’s a hard grip, knuckles up, marker still on two of them from some poster for Newman, and she holds on through it and looks straight out the windshield at Portolá’s lit windows and lets it come down her face. Jack sits on his side of the bench seat with his hands between his knees and lets her have the cab. There are Arby’s napkins in the door pocket on his side. He finds them and puts them on the seat by her leg, and eventually she takes one and holds it.
After a minute she says, in the voice she uses for procedure: “Can you leave it up on Facebook? Till I’m home? Mom first. Then Facebook. I want to tell her at the table, not on a computer.”
“Okay.”
“Eli’s going to know,” she says. “He always knows when somebody’s cried in his truck. He says it gets in the upholstery.” She folds the napkin into a square on her knee and presses it flat.
“And Theo keeps his jar.” She wipes her nose with the napkin, finally. “It isn’t *his* fault.”

body.text: “Daisy’s money’s still there if you get short for the bus.” A breath. “You can’t take my heifer. I know.”
“Daisy’s money’s still there if you get short for the bus.” A breath. “You held my hand about it. I remember.”
“Daisy’s money’s still there if you get short for the bus. That’s a Newman thing, not a girlfriend thing.”

body: Then she reaches across the seat and turns his collar down, the flannel, up on one side since the Anacapa lawn. She’s done it a hundred times. Her hand stops on it halfway, and she takes it back and puts it on the wheel.
“Go on, Jack,” she says. “I’m going to cry in Eli’s truck and you’re in it.”

response: “I’ll pray for you,” he says. “Every day.”
“I know you will.” Becca nods at the windshield. “Me too. I’m not going to stop just because.”
He opens the door, and the cold comes into the cab, and he gets out into it.

choices.text: Get out. Close the door gently.
response: He doesn’t say anything else. He gets out, and he eases the door to, slow, holding the handle out until the latch takes, so it won’t make a sound in there.
Through the glass he sees her put her forehead down on the top of the wheel.
“God bless, Becca.”

“God bless,” she says back — the way everybody says it at Coffee & Donuts at the end of every Sunday, to everybody — and for a second that’s all it is: a Sunday, and the folding tables, and the olive tree. Then he gets out into the cold.

s28c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:52 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He gets as far as the Portolá steps and sits down on them in the cold. The Ranger doesn’t move. He can hear it idling across the lot, and nothing else; without the heater in his ear the lot has its own sound, the sodium lamps humming on their poles.

body.text: While he waits he prays for her, the first of the every days, with his hands between his knees.

body: After a minute the dome light comes on in the cab. She’s reached up and switched it on herself, and he can see her small and yellow in it, bent over something on her knee. The planner, maybe. The light stays on a long time. Then, all at once, the dome light goes off.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing. Becca’s done. It’s me and the Greyhound.

body: Theo is at his desk under the lamp with a screenplay he would never call a screenplay, and he looks up when the door opens, and keeps looking. “Costigan?”
“I ended it.”

Theo closes the screenplay. He doesn’t say one clever thing. He gets up and takes his jar down off the shelf by the espresso machine — FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE, in Mrs. Lindell’s Sharpie — and works the lid until the seal gives with a small gasp, and gets two spoons out of the drawer where he keeps the good spoons, and hands Jack one.

They sit on Theo’s bed with their backs against the wall and eat huckleberry jam out of the jar. It’s sweet and sharp and tastes like somewhere colder than here. Jack is four spoonfuls in before he notices he’s eating.

body.text: “My calendar says I’m supposed to ask you something after Thanksgiving,” Theo says. “I’m going to let it wait.”

body: His iPhone lights up on the desk. He reaches over and types on it with his thumbs, quick, and sets it face down again; Jack sees the light go across the ceiling and none of the words.

body.text: Then Theo takes the Residential Services receipt out of his desk drawer, turns it over, and under $340.00 and + 1 PIE (PEACH) writes, in small square capitals: + 1 JAR (HUCKLEBERRY). FORGIVEN.

choices.text: Go to the eight o’clock confession.
response: At twenty to eight Jack stands his spoon up in the jar and gets his jacket. Theo takes custody of the jar. “Go,” he says. “I’ll guard the jam.”
choices.key: The night you ended it you went to confession. Your penance: pray for Becca by name, every day, until Advent.

response: Jack keeps his back to the wall and his spoon in his hand.
choices.key: The night you ended it you stayed in with Theo and a jar of huckleberry jam.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon.

s29a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: The confessional at St. Brendan’s was a coat closet once, and there are still hooks above the kneeler. KNOCK (gently), says the card on the door. A low lamp burns on the far side of the linen screen, and behind it Fr. Osei breathes slow and waits.

body.text: Twice in eleven days; the screen doesn’t keep count, and neither does the man behind it.

body: “I let her love me so I wouldn’t have to decide anything,” he says. “She kept showing up with things. Jam. A frame she painted. A whole plan. And I took it, and I let her think I was taking it the way she was giving it. I let her plan Christmas. I let my mother write her a letter. I knew the entire time, Father. I just didn’t say it out loud, even to me.”

The lamp hums. Fr. Osei is quiet. “My grandmother used to say the one who is carried on the back does not know how far the town is,” he says. “She carried you all fall. Now you know the distance. Good. That is where your sorrow starts, my friend. Not where it ends.”
He gives the absolution in English, unhurried, and then the penance. “Pray for her by name, every day, until Advent. Don’t skip the name.”
Out in the courtyard the olive tree is a black shape against no moon, and the broken sprinkler stands up out of the dry grass. Jack stands by the wall and says her name once. “Becca.”

Theo puts on something black and white and French — a man in a raincoat on a bridge — sets the laptop on the desk where they can both see it, and doesn’t press play. The first frame sits there with the subtitles waiting to be needed.
Two spoons in the jar. Theo takes his turn, then Jack. The jam goes down a finger. Somebody on the Lagoon path laughs at something and is gone.
Theo lies back on his pillow with his spoon. “She’s a wonderful girl.”
Jack passes him the jar.

At twenty to eleven the fourth-floor lounge has one lamp on, the one with the shade scorched brown on the side everybody keeps turned to the wall, and the window over the couch is black glass with the lamp in it. Jack is on the end of the couch with the reader open on his knee to a page he hasn’t read.

body.text: Behind him, on the half of the whiteboard the orgo kids left alone, Margot’s verdict still says BOTH, underlined, against her will.
Behind him, on the half of the whiteboard the orgo kids left alone, Margot’s verdict still says COSTIGAN — CANDLES.
Behind him, on the half of the whiteboard the orgo kids left alone, Margot’s verdict still says BROUSSARD, ON POINTS.

body: Lena comes in from the east stairs in her socks, so he doesn’t hear her until she’s in the doorway: the cardigan over flannel pajama pants printed with crawfish, thick wool socks, a Community Coffee mug held up under her chin in both hands.
“Are you okay?”
He thinks about it honestly, and gives her the only answer he’s got. “Ask me again in a week.”

It gets her. She shuts her eyes and shakes her head at him — *no, you don’t get to* — and the laugh comes anyway, short, down her nose, a sound she would clearly like back. She opens her eyes and scowls at him over the mug.
Then she comes the rest of the way in and sits on the other end of the couch with her feet tucked up under her, and holds the mug, and looks at him. “What happened?”

choices.text: “Ma wanted her at Christmas. I couldn’t take her home. I’d have been lying in my mother’s kitchen.”
choices.key: Lena came up in her socks to ask if you were okay. You told her why: you couldn’t take Becca home.
response: “Ma wanted her at Christmas,” Jack says. “I couldn’t take her home. I’d have been lying in my mother’s kitchen.”
At the other end of the couch Lena holds absolutely still, the mug under her chin. Then: “Oh, Jack.”

choices.text: “She didn’t do anything wrong. That’s the whole thing.”
response: “She didn’t do anything wrong,” Jack says. “That’s the whole thing.”
Lena nods into the mug, slowly, like it’s a point she’s conceding.

choices.text: “I hurt somebody good tonight. On purpose. Because the other thing was worse.”
response: “I hurt somebody good tonight,” Jack says. “On purpose. Because the other thing was worse.”
Lena looks at him over the mug a long time. Then she reaches along the back of the couch, not all the way to him, and leaves her hand there, palm up, in case.

choices.text: “I don’t want to talk about her. Not tonight. She’s owed that.”
response: “I don’t want to talk about her,” Jack says. “Not tonight. She’s owed that.”
“Okay,” Lena says, and drops it there.

body: “I’m sorry, Jack,” Lena says. “She’s a good girl.”

And for the next ten minutes she says every right thing there is to say. Has he eaten? He hasn’t, it turns out, unless you count a bagel at eleven and a quarter of a jar of jam on Theo’s bed, and Lena doesn’t. She digs in the cardigan pocket and comes up with half a praline in wax paper, Mémère’s, the pecans showing on the broken side.

body.text: “She says it’s for the boy with manners.”
body.else: “Don’t tell her I gave you one. She counts.”

body: He eats it. It’s so sweet it hurts his back teeth.

body.text: “Did you do it to her face?” He nods. “Good,” she says. “Most people do it on the phone.”

body: Becca will be all right, she tells him — not tonight, but she will; a girl like that has a family and a parish behind her. She’s going to tell Laney to be nice to Becca, starting tomorrow, and Laney is going to do it, because Lena will make her. He should go to the 12:10 tomorrow even if he doesn’t want to. Especially if. She’ll save him the end of a pew. She doesn’t ask about Thanksgiving. Julian doesn’t come up.
Near the end of it he remembers to ask her back. “You okay?”
“Me?” She smiles at him over the mug. “I’m fine. Thank you for asking, Jack.”
Her hand goes to the medal at her throat, under the cardigan, and comes back to the mug.

At ten to eleven she unfolds off the couch. “Get some sleep,” she says. “That isn’t a suggestion.” She sets the mug down on the lounge table to free her hands for the stairwell door, and he watches her go down the long hall toward the east stairs — the cardigan, the crawfish, the socks soundless on the linoleum, her fingers trailing along the cinderblock. At the stairwell door she stops with her hand on the bar, long enough that he thinks she’s going to turn around with one more right thing. Then she leans into it and is gone down the stairs.
The mug is still on the lounge table, full. At midnight, when he finally gets up, it’s stone cold, and he picks it up anyway and stands there holding it.

s31.slug: THURSDAY · 12:02 AM · EAST STAIRWELL → THE 2ND-FLOOR HALL
body: Jack carries Lena’s mug down the east stairs to the second floor, to the kitchenette by the elevator, and pours the coffee out — gone flat and dark, with a skin on it — and rinses the mug under the hot tap until the ring comes off, and dries it on his shirt. COMMUNITY COFFEE, it says, in red, from Louisiana.

217’s door is open about four inches. Light from inside lies across the linoleum in a stripe. Laney is standing in the gap in her PI LAM LITTLE shirt, one hand on the frame, looking back into the room at something Jack can’t see from where he is.
She turns her head and sees him. Jack doesn’t have a word for what her face is doing. Her eyes go to the mug in his hand, and back to him.
Then she closes the door, softly, all the way, without a word.
Jack stands in the hall a minute. He sets the clean mug down on the floor beside the door, the handle turned out so whoever opens it in the morning won’t kick it over.
412 is dark. Theo is sitting up in bed with his iPhone at his ear, leaving a message on a machine at twenty-five past midnight, brightly.
“Harbor Inn? Vance. Two, Saturday at eight, under Costigan. C-O-S-T-I-G-A-N. A window, if you have one, the one by the piano if you have that. Thank you *so* much.”
He hangs up and finds Jack looking at him from the other bed.

“My mother’s coming up Saturday,” Theo says. “She’s discovered rockfish. She won’t sit anywhere she can’t see a piano, and she hasn’t given her own name to a restaurant since an incident in Ojai.” Jack waits for the part where that makes sense. Theo smiles at him, pleasantly, until he stops waiting.

He plugs the phone in and lies down. On the floor between the beds the jam jar stands with two spoons in it. On Jack’s desk, by the window, Becca’s frame catches a little of the sodium light from the lawn: the two of them in the middle of it, and the painted seals going round the frame, every one of them holding on to what it weighs.
